senior.title: 🚌 Fair Public Transport: Who Gets to Move Through the City?
senior.content:
A bus map can look like a technical diagram of routes and minutes. It is also a map of opportunity. Public transport decides who can reach a job, a clinic, or a night class without owning a car, and who is left waiting in the rain at the edge of a timetable. Fairness in this system is not a luxury add-on. It is the question of whether a city moves for everyone, or mainly for those who can already afford speed and comfort. Coverage and frequency matter as much as the existence of a line. A route that appears twice a day, or that dies after early evening, cannot serve shift workers, students, or people who need to travel with children. Reliability is part of dignity: a service that is chronically late taxes the poor more heavily, because they often have less flexible employers and fewer backup options.

Price is an obvious barrier, yet so is the way fares are collected. Complicated tickets, cash-only rules, or heavy penalties for honest mistakes can exclude newcomers and the elderly. Discounts only help if people can actually obtain them. A cheap ride that is unsafe, inaccessible to wheelchairs, or impossible to understand is not truly cheap. Design and geography reveal hidden priorities. If new rail is built first for already prosperous corridors, while buses in poorer districts remain crowded and slow, investment itself becomes a form of inequality. Transit-oriented development can be a good, or it can push residents out through rising rents the moment a station arrives.

Safety, cleanliness, and the behavior of staff shape who feels entitled to ride. Women, disabled passengers, and minorities often report a different experience of the same vehicle. A fair system treats those reports as design data, not as complaints to be dismissed. Environmental arguments for public transport are strong, because a full bus or train can move people with less energy and less air pollution than a stream of private cars. Those arguments should not erase the social ones. A green policy that ignores the last mile, night service, or rural connections will still leave many people dependent on cars they can barely afford.

Students can study their own commute as a civic document: How many transfers, how much waiting, who is on the vehicle, and who is missing? The answers are a lesson in urban justice that no textbook map can fully replace. Choose one neighborhood at the edge of your city and try to plan a realistic day of work plus a clinic visit using only public transport. Note where the plan breaks. Then ask who has the power to fix that break—a budget, a timetable, a ramp, or a safer stop. Fair transport is a form of freedom that is easy for car owners to forget, and essential for anyone who cannot or should not drive.

Mobility is not only about engines and apps. It is about whether a society believes that other people’s time, safety, and destinations count as seriously as one’s own. 🚌
senior.translation:
一张公交地图看起来可能像路线和分钟的技术图解。它也是一张机会的地图。公共交通决定谁能够在没有汽车的情况下到达一份工作、一家诊所或一堂夜课，以及谁被留在时刻表边缘的雨里等待。这一系统中的公平不是奢侈的附加项。它是一个问题：一座城市是为每个人移动，还是主要为那些已经负担得起速度与舒适的人移动。 覆盖和班次与一条线路的存在同样重要。一条一天只出现两次、或一过傍晚就消失的路线，无法服务轮班工人、学生，或需要带孩子出行的人。可靠性是尊严的一部分：长期晚点的服务对穷人征税更重，因为他们的雇主往往更不灵活，备用选择也更少。

价格是明显的障碍，然而收费方式同样如此。复杂的票制、只收现金的规则，或对诚实错误的沉重处罚，可能排除新来者和老年人。折扣只有在人们真正能够获得时才有帮助。一次不安全、轮椅无法使用、或无法被理解的廉价乘坐，并不真正廉价。 设计和地理揭示隐藏的优先。如果新的轨道交通首先为已经繁荣的走廊而建，而较穷街区的公交车仍然拥挤而缓慢，投资本身就变成一种不平等。以公交为导向的开发可以是一件好事，也可以在车站到来的那一刻通过上涨的租金把居民推走。

安全、清洁和工作人员的态度塑造谁感到有权乘坐。女性、残障乘客和少数群体常常报告对同一车辆的不同体验。一个公平的系统把那些报告当作设计数据，而不是当作将被打发的抱怨。 支持公共交通的环境论据是有力的，因为满载的公交或列车可以用比一串私家车更少的能源和空气污染来运送人。那些论据不应当抹去社会论据。一项忽视最后一公里、夜间服务或乡村连接的绿色政策，仍将使许多人依赖他们几乎负担不起的汽车。

学生可以把他们自己的通勤当成一份公民文件来研究：多少次换乘，多少等待，车上是谁，谁又缺席？这些答案是一堂城市正义课，没有教科书上的地图能够完全替代。 选择你所在城市边缘的一个街区，试着只用公共交通安排现实的一天：上班再加上一次诊所就诊。记下计划在哪里破裂。然后再问谁有权力修复那一破裂——一笔预算、一张时刻表、一道坡道，或一个更安全的车站。公平的交通是一种车主容易忘记、而对不能或不应当开车的人却必不可少的自由。

流动性不仅仅与引擎和应用程序有关。它关系到一个社会是否相信：别人的时间、安全和目的地，与自己的同样算数。 🚌

senior.title: 😊 Happiness Economics: What We Miss When We Count Only Money
senior.content:
Gross domestic product was designed to measure the size of an economy, not the quality of a life. It remains a useful tool, and it is a poor substitute for asking whether people are healthy, trusted, and able to spend time with those they love. Happiness economics, or more cautiously the study of well-being, tries to bring those questions into public debate without pretending that a smile can be taxed like income. The aim is not to outlaw ambition, but to notice what a money-only scoreboard leaves out. Surveys of life satisfaction, measures of mental health, and data on social connection often tell a different story from a rising national income. In some places, extra wealth after a certain point buys less additional happiness than people expect, especially if inequality, long hours, or insecure work rise at the same time. The pattern is debated, which is healthy; the invitation to look beyond GDP should not depend on one famous graph.

Governments that take well-being seriously may invest more visibly in parks, mental-health care, cleaner air, and time—through leave policies or limits on crushing overtime. They may also become tempted to treat happiness as a slogan, or to cherry-pick numbers that flatter their rule. Measurement can serve citizens, or it can become a new kind of public relations. Critics warn that happiness is subjective, culturally shaped, and easy to manipulate with leading questions. They are right that no single index should replace democratic argument. Supporters reply that “hard” economic numbers are also full of choices: what counts as production, whose unpaid care is ignored, and how environmental damage is priced, if it is priced at all.

There is a personal side that should not be confused with policy. A student can ask what actually improves a week of life—sleep, friendship, useful work, a walk—without waiting for a ministry. Yet individual tips cannot fix a city with no safe parks or a job that allows no rest. Well-being is both a private skill and a public condition. Inequality complicates the picture. Average happiness can hide a miserable minority, just as average income can. A serious approach looks at distributions, at children and the elderly, and at whether people feel they have a voice, not only at a national mean.

The deepest contribution of this field may be cultural. It gives permission to say that a society can be busy and still be failing, if trust is thin and time is always for sale. Compare a headline about economic growth with what you can learn about sleep, loneliness, or air quality in the same year. Then decide what you would want a government to report alongside GDP. Happiness economics is most useful when it remains a set of questions, not a new religion of numbers. It asks us to be precise about the kind of prosperity we are actually trying to build.

Money is a powerful servant and a limited portrait. Counting well-being will not make hard choices disappear, but it can stop us from mistaking a thicker wallet for a complete success. 😊
senior.translation:
国内生产总值被设计来衡量一个经济的规模，而不是一种生活的质量。它仍然是有用的工具，却是询问人们是否健康、被信任、并能够与所爱的人共度时间的糟糕替代品。幸福经济学，或更谨慎地说对福祉的研究，试图把这些问题带进公共辩论，而不假装一个微笑可以像收入一样被征税。目的不是禁止雄心，而是注意到一个只看金钱的记分牌遗漏了什么。 生活满意度调查、心理健康测量以及社会连接的数据，常常讲述一个与不断上升的国民收入不同的故事。在一些地方，超过某一点之后的额外财富，带来的额外幸福比人们预期的更少，尤其当不平等、长工时或不稳定工作同时上升时。这一模式存在争论，这是健康的；超越 GDP 去看的邀请，不应当依赖于一张著名的图。

认真对待福祉的政府，可能更明显地投资于公园、心理健康护理、更清洁的空气，以及时间——通过休假政策或对压垮性加班的限制。它们也可能受到诱惑，把幸福当成口号，或挑选奉承其统治的数字。测量可以为公民服务，也可以变成一种新的公共关系。 批评者警告，幸福是主观的，受文化塑造，并且容易被诱导性问题操纵。他们是对的：没有任何单一指数应当取代民主争论。支持者回应，“硬”经济数字同样充满选择：什么算作生产，谁的无酬照护被忽略，以及环境损害如何被定价——如果它被定价的话。

有个人的一面不应当与政策混淆。一个学生可以询问什么真正改善一周的生活——睡眠、友谊、有用的工作、一次散步——而不必等待一个部委。然而个人技巧不能修复一座没有安全公园的城市，或一份不允许休息的工作。福祉既是私人技能，也是公共条件。 不平等使图景复杂化。平均幸福可以隐藏痛苦的少数，正如平均收入可以。严肃的方法会看分布，看儿童和老人，看人们是否感到自己拥有声音，而不仅仅看一个全国平均数。

这一领域最深的贡献可能是文化上的。它给出许可，去说一个社会可以很忙碌却仍然在失败，如果信任稀薄，而时间总是待价而沽。 把一条关于经济增长的标题，与你在同一年里能够了解的睡眠、孤独或空气质量相比较。然后决定你希望政府在 GDP 之外还报告什么。幸福经济学在仍然是一组问题、而不是一种新的数字宗教时最有用。它要求我们精确说明：我们实际上正在试图建造的是哪一种繁荣。

金钱是强大的仆人，也是有限的肖像。计算福祉不会使艰难的选择消失，但它可以阻止我们把更厚的钱包误当成一次完全的成功。 😊

questions.q: 1. Why is GDP called a poor substitute for well-being?
options: Because smiles can be taxed like income
Because it cannot measure any economic activity
Because ambition should be outlawed
Because it was designed to measure the size of an economy, not whether people are healthy, trusted, and able to spend time with those they love
questions.exp: GDP 衡量经济规模，而不能代替对健康、信任和与所爱者共处时间的询问。

questions.q: 2. What caution is offered about governments that report happiness?
options: They cannot be tempted by slogans
They must replace all democratic argument with one index
They may treat it as a slogan or cherry-pick flattering numbers; measurement can become public relations
They should never invest in parks or mental-health care
questions.exp: 政府可能把幸福当口号或挑选奉承数字，测量会变成公关。

questions.q: 3. How do supporters answer the claim that happiness is too subjective?
options: By saying “hard” economic numbers are also full of choices about production, unpaid care, and environmental damage
By ignoring inequality and distributions
By treating a single graph as a religion
By denying that culture shapes answers
questions.exp: “硬”经济数字同样充满关于生产、无酬照护和环境定价的选择。

questions.q: 4. Why is well-being both a private skill and a public condition?
options: Because averages never hide a miserable minority
Because time is never for sale
Because tips about sleep and friendship matter, yet they cannot fix a city with no safe parks or a job with no rest
Because ministries can replace all personal habits
questions.exp: 个人习惯重要，但不能修复没有安全公园的城市或不允许休息的工作。

questions.q: 5. What comparison is suggested to the student?
options: Assume extra wealth always buys as much happiness as expected
Compare a growth headline with sleep, loneliness, or air quality in the same year, and decide what else should be reported beside GDP
Wait for a ministry before asking what improves a week
Count only wallets as complete success
questions.exp: 把增长标题与同年的睡眠、孤独或空气质量比较，并决定 GDP 之外还应报告什么。

senior.title: 🔓 Open Science: Why Knowledge Should Be Easier to Check, Share, and Correct
senior.content:
Science advertises itself as a self-correcting public enterprise, yet much of its daily machinery has been closed: paywalled papers, hidden data, and methods described too briefly to repeat. Open science is a movement to make evidence, materials, and sometimes even laboratory notebooks more available, so that claims can be checked by people who were not in the original room. The goal is not exhibitionism. It is to make the advertised virtue of science more nearly true. Replication is difficult when a paper reports a striking result but not the messy path that produced it. Sharing data, code, and detailed protocols allows others to test whether a finding is solid, limited, or a product of flexible analysis. This can be embarrassing for authors, and it is a form of respect for readers and for future patients or policymakers who may act on the result.

Open access publishing tries to remove the absurdity of the public, or universities, paying twice—once to fund the work and again to read it. The model is still evolving, and new fees can burden authors who lack grants. “Open” that merely shifts costs onto poorer laboratories is an incomplete reform. Preprints, which are papers posted before formal peer review, can speed discussion in a fast-moving field, as the world saw during recent health emergencies. They can also spread errors if journalists and social media treat them as finished truth. Openness needs a literate audience, not only a faster server.

There are legitimate limits. Some data involve personal privacy, endangered species, or security. Intellectual property and the careers of young researchers who fear being scooped are real concerns. Thoughtful open science designs exceptions and credit, rather than demanding that everything be posted instantly and without protection. Culture may be harder to change than tools. Journals, hiring committees, and funders still often reward novelty and quantity more than careful sharing and negative results. Until those incentives move, openness will remain a hobby of the conscientious rather than the default of the system.

Students can practice the spirit of the idea on a small scale: citing sources they have actually seen, showing their working, and distinguishing a preliminary claim from a confirmed one. Open science begins as a habit of intellectual honesty, not only as a global policy. Pick a popular science headline and try to reach the underlying paper or dataset. Notice the barriers—price, jargon, missing files—and ask who those barriers serve. Then read whether the authors shared enough for someone else to check them. The exercise turns “trust science” from a slogan into a practical demand: trust is easier when the work can be seen.

A result that cannot be inspected is only a rumor with better stationery. Opening science is a way of keeping a powerful institution answerable to the same curiosity that created it. 🔓
senior.translation:
科学把自己宣传为一项自我纠正的公共事业，然而它的许多日常机器却是封闭的：付费墙后的论文、隐藏的数据，以及描述得太简略以至于无法重复的方法。开放科学是一场运动，旨在使证据、材料，有时甚至实验室笔记更加可获得，以便那些并不在原初房间里的人能够检查主张。目标不是出风头。而是使科学所宣传的美德更接近真实。 当一篇论文报告一个惊人结果，却不报告产生它的杂乱路径时，重复就很困难。分享数据、代码和详细规程，允许他人测试一项发现是坚实的、有限的，还是灵活分析的产物。这对作者可能令人尴尬，却是对读者、以及对可能依据该结果行动的未来病人或政策制定者的一种尊重。

开放获取出版试图消除公众或大学付两次钱的荒谬——一次资助工作，再一次阅读它。这一模式仍在演变，新的费用可能加重缺乏经费的作者的负担。仅仅把成本转移到较穷实验室的“开放”，是一次不完整的改革。 预印本，即在正式同行评审之前张贴的论文，可以在一个快速变动的领域加快讨论，正如世界在近来的卫生紧急情况中所见。如果记者和社交媒体把它们当成完成的真理，它们也可能传播错误。开放需要有素养的受众，而不仅仅是一台更快的服务器。

存在正当的限度。有些数据涉及个人隐私、濒危物种或安全。知识产权，以及担心被抢先的年轻研究者的职业，都是真实的关切。深思熟虑的开放科学设计例外和认可，而不是要求一切都被立刻、毫无保护地张贴。 文化可能比工具更难改变。期刊、招聘委员会和资助方仍然常常比仔细的分享和阴性结果更奖励新奇和数量。直到那些激励移动，开放将仍是有良心者的爱好，而不是系统的默认。

学生可以在小尺度上练习这一想法的精神：引用他们真正看过的来源，展示他们的过程，并区分初步主张与已被确认的主张。开放科学始于智识诚实的习惯，而不仅仅是一项全球政策。 选一条热门科学标题，试着到达其背后的论文或数据集。注意那些障碍——价格、行话、缺失的文件——并询问这些障碍为谁服务。然后再看作者是否分享了足够的内容，好让别人能够检查他们。这个练习把“相信科学”从一句口号变成一项实际要求：当工作能够被看见时，信任更容易。

一个无法被检查的结果，只是一张更好信纸上的谣言。开放科学，是让一个强大的机构对造就了它的同一种好奇心负责的方式。 🔓

questions.q: 1. What is the goal of open science, as stated here?
options: To make evidence and materials more available so claims can be checked by people who were not in the original room
To abolish all privacy and security limits
Exhibitionism about laboratory notebooks
To hide data and shorten methods further
questions.exp: 使证据和材料更可获得，以便原房间之外的人能够检查主张。

questions.q: 2. Why does sharing data and code matter for replication?
options: It always embarrasses readers rather than authors
It proves that paywalls improve checking
It allows others to test whether a finding is solid, limited, or a product of flexible analysis
It replaces the need to respect future patients
questions.exp: 分享数据、代码和规程，让他人检验发现是否坚实、有限或来自灵活分析。

questions.q: 3. What risk of preprints is mentioned?
options: Journalists and social media may treat them as finished truth and spread errors
They always complete peer review first
They require no literate audience
They can never speed discussion in an emergency
questions.exp: 若被当成完成的真理，预印本可能传播错误。

questions.q: 4. Why might culture be harder to change than tools?
options: Because openness is already the system’s default
Because incentives have already fully moved
Because journals and funders still often reward novelty and quantity more than careful sharing and negative results
Because young researchers never fear being scooped
questions.exp: 期刊和资助方仍常更奖励新奇与数量，而非仔细分享和阴性结果。

questions.q: 5. What should a student do with a popular science headline?
options: Ignore jargon, prices, and missing files
Trust the headline as a finished result
Treat “trust science” as a slogan that needs no inspection
Try to reach the paper or dataset, notice barriers, and ask whether enough was shared to be checked
questions.exp: 尝试到达论文或数据，注意障碍，并询问是否分享了足够内容以供检查。

senior.title: 🎒 Education for Refugee Students: Learning When Home Has Been Interrupted
senior.content:
A classroom assumes a great deal that is easy to forget: a stable address, a known language of instruction, records of past study, and a mind not occupied by fear. Refugee students often arrive with talent and with none of those assumptions intact. Education in this setting is not a soft extra after food and shelter. It is one of the few tools that can restore a future, protect children from exploitation, and help a host community live with newcomers as more than a temporary emergency. The first barriers are practical. Families may lack documents that prove a child’s age or previous grade. Schools may be full, far away, or legally closed to people without a certain status. Even when a place is offered, uniforms, transport, and the cost of materials can quietly exclude. A right that exists only on paper is not yet a right in the morning timetable.

Language is both a bridge and a wall. Students need support in the language of the new school without being treated as empty of knowledge they already have. A teenager who has studied algebra in another tongue is not a beginner in thinking. Programs that only place older children in the lowest class can waste years and damage dignity. Trauma and interrupted schooling shape attention. Some students need counseling and patience more than they need another test; others are hungry to catch up and should not be defined only as victims. Teachers require training and smaller loads, which host systems under pressure often cannot provide without outside help and political will.

Inclusion benefits the receiving class as well, if it is planned. Children learn that a classmate’s story may be larger than a headline, and that languages can sit side by side. Poorly planned inclusion, by contrast, can produce crowding, resentment, and a story that “they” lowered standards. The failure is then blamed on the newcomers rather than on the missing resources. Longer-term policy matters because displacement can last for years. Temporary classrooms that never connect to recognized qualifications leave young people in a corridor with no door. Pathways into secondary school, vocational training, and university must be designed early, not improvised when a child turns eighteen.

There is a moral test for wealthy countries and for neighbors that already host the largest numbers. Responsibility should not fall only on the poorest places simply because they are closest to a conflict. Education is part of a shared obligation, not a local accident of geography. If your school has new classmates from another country, notice what would help you if the situation were reversed: a glossary, a buddy, a teacher who does not rush, a way to show what you already know. If your school has no such students, follow one reputable report on a camp or a host city and look for the educational details, not only the political argument. Refugee education is a measure of whether we believe childhood can continue after a border has been crossed in fear.

A desk, a language, and a recognized certificate may look ordinary from a comfortable seat. For a student whose life has been interrupted, they can be the first solid ground in a new map of the world. 🎒
senior.translation:
一间教室假定了许多容易被忘记的东西：一个稳定的地址、一种已知的教学语言、过去学习的记录，以及一颗不被恐惧占据的心。难民学生常常带着才能到来，却没有这些完整的假定。在这种情境中，教育不是食物和住所之后的柔软附加。它是少数能够恢复未来、保护儿童免受剥削，并帮助接收社区把新来者当作不仅是一场临时紧急事件来相处的工具之一。 第一批障碍是实际的。家庭可能缺少证明孩子年龄或先前年级的文件。学校可能已经满员、距离很远，或在法律上对没有某种身份的人关闭。即使提供了一个名额，校服、交通和材料费用也可能悄悄排除。一项只存在于纸上的权利，还不是早晨时刻表里的权利。

语言既是桥，也是墙。学生需要在新学校的语言上得到支持，而不被当成没有他们已有知识的空容器。一个用另一种语言学过代数的少年，并不是思维上的初学者。只把年龄较大的孩子放进最低班级的项目，可能浪费岁月并损害尊严。 创伤和被打断的学业塑造注意力。有些学生需要咨询和耐心，多于他们需要又一次考试；另一些人急于赶上，不应当只被定义成受害者。教师需要训练和更小的负荷，而承压的接收体系若没有外部帮助和政治意愿，往往无法提供这些。

如果计划得当，包容也使接收班级受益。孩子们会学到，一位同学的故事可能比一条标题更大，语言可以并肩而坐。相比之下，计划不良的包容可能产生拥挤、怨恨，以及“他们”降低了标准的故事。失败随后被归咎于新来者，而不是归咎于缺失的资源。 长期政策很重要，因为流离可以持续多年。从不连接到被承认资格的临时教室，把年轻人留在一条没有门的走廊里。进入中学、职业训练和大学的路径必须及早设计，而不是在一个孩子年满十八岁时临时拼凑。

对富裕国家，以及对已经接收最大数量难民的邻国，这是一项道德检验。责任不应当仅仅因为最穷的地方最靠近冲突就落在它们身上。教育是共享义务的一部分，不是地理上的地方意外。 如果你的学校有来自另一个国家的新同学，注意如果情形对调，什么会帮助你：一份词汇表、一个伙伴、一位不催促的老师、一种展示你已有知识的方式。如果你的学校没有这样的学生，跟随一篇关于难民营或接收城市的可靠报道，寻找教育上的细节，而不仅仅是政治争论。难民教育是一种衡量：我们是否相信，在恐惧中越过边界之后，童年仍可以继续。

一张书桌、一种语言和一份被承认的证书，从舒适的座位上看起来可能很普通。对一个生命已被打断的学生，它们可以是新世界地图上的第一块坚实土地。 🎒

senior.title: 🏠 Indoor Air: The Pollution We Breathe Without Going Outside
senior.content:
Public debate about air quality often stops at the street: traffic, factories, and a haze on the horizon. Many people, however, spend most of their hours indoors, where the air can be worse than the air outside. Cooking smoke, damp, cleaning chemicals, old paint, poorly vented heaters, and a lack of fresh-air exchange can turn a room into a private atmosphere with public consequences. Indoor air is a health issue that hides in ordinary life, which is why it is so easy to ignore. The sources are diverse. In some homes, solid-fuel stoves or poorly maintained gas appliances release particles and carbon monoxide. In others, the problems are mold in wet walls, formaldehyde from cheap furniture, or radon seeping from the ground. Tobacco smoke, if present, remains one of the most damaging indoor pollutants, including for people who never chose to smoke.

Ventilation is the unglamorous hero. A tightly sealed building may save energy and still trap pollutants and moisture unless it is designed with proper air exchange. Opening a window helps in many situations, but it is not a complete strategy in a noisy, cold, or highly polluted street, or in a room that has no window to open. Schools and offices deserve as much attention as houses. Crowded classrooms with low fresh-air flow can raise the risk of infection and can make thinking harder, as anyone who has sat in a stuffy exam hall already suspects. After recent years of attention to airborne disease, it would be a waste to forget the lesson the moment the emergency fades.

The burden is uneven. Renters may be unable to fix a moldy wall or a dangerous heater; informal housing may lack safe chimneys; children and the elderly spend more time inside and are more vulnerable. An indoor problem is often a housing-rights problem wearing a medical mask. Solutions include cleaner cooking fuels, exhaust fans, moisture control, bans on indoor smoking, radon testing, and building standards that treat ventilation as essential, not as an afterthought. Individuals can reduce some risks, but landlords, schools, and regulators hold larger keys.

Students can treat their own rooms as a small field study: Where does steam go after a shower? Is there a smell of damp or of strong cleaners? Does anyone sleep in a room with a heater that has no vent? The questions are humble and can be life-saving. Ask a science teacher or a public-health page how carbon monoxide is detected, and whether your home or school has a working alarm. Then look at who in your city is most likely to live with damp or with cooking smoke. Indoor air links chemistry to justice. A society that only measures the sky outside the window may miss the air that is actually in people’s lungs while they sleep.

The air indoors is not a private luxury or a purely personal taste. It is part of the public health of a country, as real as a river, and closer than most people think. 🏠
senior.translation:
关于空气质量的公共辩论常常停在街上：交通、工厂和地平线上的一层霾。然而许多人把大部分时间花在室内，那里的空气可能比外面更差。烹饪烟雾、潮湿、清洁化学品、旧油漆、通风不良的加热器，以及缺乏新鲜空气交换，可以把一个房间变成一种具有公共后果的私人大气。室内空气是一个隐藏在普通生活中的健康问题，这正是它如此容易被忽视的原因。 来源是多样的。在一些家庭，固体燃料炉或维护不良的燃气器具释放颗粒物和一氧化碳。在另一些家庭，问题是湿墙里的霉菌、廉价家具中的甲醛，或从地下渗入的氡。如果存在烟草烟雾，它仍是最具损害性的室内污染物之一，包括对从未选择吸烟的人。

通风是不起眼的英雄。一座密封很紧的建筑可能节约能源，却仍会困住污染物和湿气，除非它被设计了适当的空气交换。开窗在许多情况下有帮助，但在嘈杂、寒冷或户外污染严重的街道上，或在一个没有窗可开的房间里，它并不是完整的策略。 学校和办公室应当得到与住宅同样多的注意。新鲜空气流动低的拥挤教室可能提高感染风险，并可能使思考更难，任何在闷热考场里坐过的人已经怀疑这一点。在近年来对空气传播疾病的关注之后，一旦紧急状态消退就忘记这一课，将是一种浪费。

负担并不均匀。租客可能无法修理发霉的墙或危险的加热器；非正规住房可能缺少安全的烟囱；儿童和老人在室内的时间更多，也更脆弱。一个室内问题常常是一个戴着医用口罩的住房权利问题。 解决办法包括更清洁的烹饪燃料、排气扇、湿度控制、禁止室内吸烟、氡检测，以及把通风当作必要而非事后想法的建筑标准。个人可以降低某些风险，但房东、学校和监管者握有更大的钥匙。

学生可以把他们自己的房间当成一项小小的田野研究：淋浴后的蒸汽去了哪里？是否有潮湿或强烈清洁剂的气味？是否有人在没有通风的加热器旁睡觉？这些问题是谦逊的，却可以救命。 向科学老师或公共卫生页面询问一氧化碳如何被检测，以及你的家或学校是否有正在工作的警报器。然后再看在你的城市里，谁最可能与潮湿或烹饪烟雾住在一起。室内空气把化学与正义联系起来。一个只测量窗外天空的社会，可能错过人们睡觉时真正在肺里的空气。

室内的空气不是私人奢侈，也不是纯粹的个人趣味。它是一个国家公共卫生的一部分，与一条河同样真实，并且比大多数人以为的更近。 🏠

senior.title: 🏅 Sports Science: Training Smarter Without Treating Athletes as Machines
senior.content:
Victory in sport is still decided by a body in motion, but the path to that motion is increasingly shaped by data: oxygen use, sleep charts, biomechanics, and carefully planned recovery. Sports science can protect athletes from crude overtraining and can raise the ceiling of performance. It can also turn a person into a dashboard, and a childhood game into an industry of measurement. The useful question is not whether science belongs in sport, but how it can serve health and fairness rather than only the next record. Physiology explains why interval training, periodization, and rest days work better than endless identical sessions. The body adapts to stress and then needs time to rebuild; more is not always more. Coaches who understand this can reduce injuries and improve results, especially in young athletes whose bones and minds are still developing.

Nutrition, hydration, and sleep are now treated as training, not as afterthoughts. That is progress, provided it does not become an anxious religion of grams and gadgets. An amateur runner can benefit from simple habits; an elite athlete may need specialist support. The same poster should not be pasted on every locker. Technology has entered the field in the form of wearables, video analysis, and sometimes genetic or medical testing. These tools can reveal a weakness in a stride or a risky pattern of workload. They also raise questions about privacy, about pressure to train through pain, and about whether wealthy clubs will widen the gap simply by buying better science.

Ethics is not an outsider to the laboratory. Doping is the most obvious betrayal of fair competition and of the athlete’s long-term health. Less obvious are methods that sit in a grey zone, or medical practices that return a player to the field before a brain or a joint has recovered. A team doctor’s first patient should be the person, not the fixture list. Gender, disability, and age categories show that “the same rules for everyone” can be complicated when bodies differ. Sports science can inform those debates with evidence, but it cannot replace values about inclusion and safety. Numbers describe; they do not by themselves decide who is allowed to play.

For students who love a sport, the healthiest lesson may be this: listen to data without surrendering your own signals of pain and joy. A clever plan that destroys the reason you started is not clever enough. Watch one training session, or your own, and note what is being measured and what is being ignored: mood, friendship, a sore knee, the pleasure of a well-timed pass. Then read one reliable explanation of why rest matters. Sports science is most impressive when it makes athletes more durable and more human, not merely more optimized for a single season.

A record is a fact, and a career is a life. The science of sport earns its keep when it remembers the difference, and when it refuses to treat the body as a tool that can be replaced after the final whistle. 🏅
senior.translation:
体育中的胜利仍然由一个运动中的身体决定，但通向那一运动的道路正日益被数据塑造：氧气使用、睡眠图表、生物力学，以及仔细计划的恢复。运动科学可以保护运动员免于粗放的过度训练，并可以提高表现的上限。它也可以把一个人变成一块仪表盘，把童年的游戏变成一场测量工业。有用的问题不是科学是否属于体育，而是它如何能够服务健康与公平，而不仅仅是下一项纪录。 生理学解释了为什么间歇训练、周期化和休息日，比无尽的相同课次更有效。身体适应压力，然后需要时间重建；更多并不总是更多。理解这一点的教练可以减少伤病并改善成绩，尤其是对骨骼和心智仍在发育的年轻运动员。

营养、补水和睡眠现在被当作训练，而不是事后想法。这是进步，只要它不变成一种关于克数和装置的焦虑宗教。业余跑者可以从简单习惯中受益；精英运动员可能需要专家支持。同一张海报不应当被贴在每一个储物柜上。 技术以可穿戴设备、视频分析，有时还有基因或医学检测的形式进入了这个领域。这些工具可以揭示步态中的弱点或危险的负荷模式。它们也提出关于隐私、关于带伤训练的压力，以及富裕俱乐部是否会仅仅通过购买更好的科学来扩大差距的问题。

伦理并不是实验室的局外人。兴奋剂是对公平竞争和运动员长期健康最明显的背叛。不那么明显的，是处于灰色地带的方法，或在大脑或关节恢复之前就把球员送回场地的医疗做法。队医的第一位病人应当是那个人，而不是赛程表。 性别、残疾和年龄组别表明，当身体不同时，“对每个人同样的规则”可能变得复杂。运动科学可以用证据为这些辩论提供信息，但它不能替代关于包容与安全的价值。数字描述；它们并不能独自决定谁被允许比赛。

对热爱一项运动的学生，最健康的课可能是这个：倾听数据，而不交出你自己关于疼痛与喜悦的信号。一个毁掉你开始原因的聪明计划，还不够聪明。 观看一次训练，或你自己的训练，注意什么正在被测量，什么正在被忽略：心情、友谊、隐痛的膝盖、一次时机正好的传球的愉快。然后再读一篇关于为什么休息重要的可靠解释。当运动科学使运动员更耐久、也更像人，而不仅仅为单一赛季更优化时，它才最令人印象深刻。

一项纪录是一个事实，而一份职业生涯是一条生命。当运动科学记得这一差别，并拒绝把身体当成终场哨响后可以被替换的工具时，它才配得上自己的位置。 🏅

senior.title: 🌿 Traditional Knowledge: Wisdom That Did Not Begin in a Laboratory
senior.content:
Modern science is a powerful method, not the only library of human intelligence. Across the world, communities have developed detailed knowledge of plants, animals, weather, soils, and healing through long observation and practice. This traditional or indigenous knowledge is sometimes dismissed as folklore, and sometimes romantically treated as automatically perfect. Both reactions are lazy. The serious task is to listen carefully, test claims fairly, and protect the rights of the people who have kept the knowledge alive. Examples are easy to find and easy to oversimplify. Agricultural calendars, navigation by stars and currents, fire management, and the uses of particular plants have often proved precise in their own landscapes. When such knowledge is ignored, development projects can fail, and ecosystems can be damaged by “improvements” that do not understand a place.

Problems arise when companies or researchers collect local expertise and then patent or publish it without consent or benefit-sharing. This is not a quarrel about nostalgia; it is a quarrel about justice and about who is allowed to profit from a discovery. Codes of conduct and legal tools now exist in some places, but they are unevenly enforced. Traditional knowledge is also not frozen. It changes as climates change, as trade arrives, and as younger people choose what to learn. Treating it as a museum exhibit can be a polite way of letting it die. Support for language, land rights, and intergenerational teaching matters more than a single documentary.

Science and traditional knowledge can complement each other when neither side assumes it already owns the whole truth. Rangers and elders have helped locate species; healers have pointed chemists toward compounds, provided the relationship is respectful. Conflict appears when one system insists on being the only judge, or when spiritual meanings are stripped away as if they were packaging. Schools can include local knowledge without turning it into a costume day. Students might map seasonal signs, learn a plant’s name in a local language, and also learn how a scientific test works. The point is intellectual respect, not a contest to see which system can mock the other.

Skepticism remains necessary. Some traditional claims, like some scientific ones, are wrong or harmful. The standard should be evidence and harm, applied consistently, not a double rule that excuses everything ancient or everything published in English. Ask whether your region has ecological or medical knowledge that rarely appears in textbooks, and who still holds it. If you can listen, do so with permission and without treating the speaker as a tourist attraction. Traditional knowledge is a reminder that intelligence has many addresses, and that a fair society does not steal from the oldest libraries just because they were not written in the format a university prefers.

A laboratory is one way of knowing. A landscape watched for generations is another. The future will be poorer if we can only respect the first, or if we can only praise the second and never ask a careful question. 🌿
senior.translation:
现代科学是一种强大的方法，却不是人类智慧的唯一图书馆。在世界各地，社区通过长期观察和实践，发展了关于植物、动物、天气、土壤和治疗的细致知识。这种传统或原住民知识有时被当成民间传说打发掉，有时又被浪漫地当成自动完美。两种反应都是懒惰的。严肃的任务是仔细倾听，公平地检验主张，并保护那些使知识活下来的人的权利。 例子很容易找到，也很容易被过度简化。农业历法、靠星星和洋流的航海、火的管理，以及特定植物的用途，在它们自己的土地上常常被证明是精确的。当这类知识被忽视，发展项目可能失败，生态系统也可能被并不理解一个地方的“改进”所损害。

当公司或研究者收集本地专长，然后在未经同意或不分享利益的情况下申请专利或发表时，问题就出现了。这不是一场关于怀旧的争吵；这是一场关于正义、以及谁被允许从一项发现中获利的争吵。行为准则和法律工具现在在一些地方存在，但执行并不均匀。 传统知识也不是冻结的。它随着气候改变、贸易到来，以及年轻人选择学习什么而变化。把它当成博物馆展品，可能是一种让它死去的礼貌方式。对语言、土地权利和代际教学的支持，比一部纪录片更重要。

当双方都不假定自己已经拥有全部真理时，科学与传统知识可以互相补充。护林员和长者帮助定位过物种；治疗者曾为化学家指向化合物，只要关系是尊重的。当一个体系坚持成为唯一的法官，或当精神意义被当作包装剥掉时，冲突就会出现。 学校可以纳入本地知识，而不把它变成化装日。学生可以绘制季节信号，学习一种植物在本地语言中的名字，同时也学习科学测试如何运作。要点是智识上的尊重，而不是一场看哪个体系更能嘲笑对方的竞赛。

怀疑仍然必要。一些传统主张，像一些科学主张一样，是错误或有害的。标准应当是证据与伤害，被一贯地应用，而不是一套为一切古老之物或一切用英文发表之物开脱的双重规则。 询问你所在的地区是否有很少出现在课本里的生态或医学知识，以及谁仍然持有它。如果你能够倾听，请带着许可去听，而不要把讲述者当成旅游景点。传统知识提醒我们，智慧有许多地址；一个公平的社会不会仅仅因为最古老的图书馆不是以大学偏好的格式写成，就从它们那里偷走东西。

实验室是一种认识方式。被世代观看的土地是另一种。如果我们只能尊重前者，或只能赞美后者而从不提出一个仔细的问题，未来将更为贫乏。 🌿

senior.title: 💧 Hydrogen as Energy: A Flexible Fuel That Is Only as Clean as Its Origin
senior.content:
Hydrogen is the most abundant element in the universe, and on Earth it is almost always bound to other atoms. As a fuel or a store of energy, it can produce electricity in a fuel cell or burn with water as the main chemical product, which makes it sound like a perfect climate solution. The difficulty is hidden in the adjectives. Hydrogen is only as clean as the method used to produce it, and only as practical as the tanks, pipelines, and costs that surround it. Most hydrogen today is made from natural gas, a process that releases carbon dioxide unless the carbon is captured—an expensive and incomplete fix. Hydrogen made by splitting water with electricity is cleaner if the electricity itself is renewable or otherwise low-carbon, and wasteful if the electricity comes from coal. Color labels such as “grey,” “blue,” and “green” are shorthand for these origins, not proof of automatic virtue.

Hydrogen is useful where batteries struggle: some kinds of heavy transport, high-temperature industry, and long-duration storage. It is less convincing as a way to heat every home or to replace every car, because conversion losses are large and infrastructure is costly. A serious energy strategy matches the tool to the job rather than advertising a single molecule as a universal hero. Safety and leakage matter. Hydrogen is flammable and can escape from pipes more easily than some other gases; it is also an indirect greenhouse issue if it leaks in large amounts, because it affects other gases in the atmosphere. Engineering can reduce these risks, but slogans cannot.

Geopolitics will change if hydrogen trade grows. Countries with cheap renewable power may export it, new pipelines may create dependencies, and workers in old fuel industries will need a just transition. A technology that only relocates fossil influence under a new name would be a disappointing revolution. Public debate should therefore ask boring, essential questions. How was this hydrogen made? How much energy was lost along the way? Who pays for the infrastructure, and who benefits? Without those questions, “hydrogen economy” becomes a phrase that can greenwash almost anything.

Students can compare a hydrogen plan with a battery plan for a specific use—a city bus, a steel plant, a winter week of still air—and list advantages honestly. The exercise trains resistance to magic-word energy policy. When you see an advertisement for a hydrogen car or a “green factory,” look for the electricity or gas behind the fuel. If the text is silent, the silence is information. Hydrogen can be part of a cleaner system, but only if we remain more loyal to carbon numbers than to fashionable molecules.

A fuel is not a moral category; it is a chain of transformations. Hydrogen will help the climate if that chain is clean, careful, and reserved for the work it can actually do well. 💧
senior.translation:
氢是宇宙中最丰富的元素，而在地球上它几乎总是与其他原子结合。作为燃料或能量储存，它可以在燃料电池中产生电，或燃烧并以水为主要化学产物，这使它听起来像完美的气候解决方案。困难隐藏在形容词里。氢只有与生产它的方法一样清洁，也只有与围绕它的储罐、管道和成本一样实用。 今天大部分氢来自天然气，这一过程会释放二氧化碳，除非碳被捕捉——这是一种昂贵且不完整的修补。用电力分解水制成的氢，如果电本身是可再生或其他低碳的，就会更清洁；如果电来自煤，则是浪费的。“灰”“蓝”“绿”这类颜色标签是这些来源的速记，不是自动美德的证明。

氢在电池吃力的地方有用：某些重型运输、高温工业和长时储能。作为给每一户供暖或替换每一辆汽车的方式，它不那么令人信服，因为转换损失大，基础设施昂贵。严肃的能源战略把工具匹配到工作上，而不是把一个分子宣传成万能英雄。 安全与泄漏很重要。氢是易燃的，并且比某些其他气体更容易从管道逃逸；如果大量泄漏，它也是一个间接的温室问题，因为它会影响大气中的其他气体。工程可以降低这些风险，但口号不能。

如果氢贸易增长，地缘政治将会改变。拥有廉价可再生电力的国家可能出口它，新的管道可能制造依赖，而旧燃料产业中的工人将需要公正转型。一项仅仅在新名称下重新安置化石影响的技术，将是一场令人失望的革命。 公共辩论因此应当提出乏味而必要的问题。这些氢是如何制成的？沿途损失了多少能量？谁为基础设施付钱，谁又受益？没有这些问题，“氢经济”就会变成一个几乎可以给任何东西洗绿的短语。

学生可以把一个氢计划与一个电池计划就特定用途进行比较——一辆城市公交、一座钢厂、一个无风的冬季星期——并诚实地列出优势。这个练习训练对“魔法词”能源政策的抵抗。 当你看见一则氢能汽车或“绿色工厂”的广告时，寻找燃料背后的电或天然气。如果文字保持沉默，沉默本身就是信息。氢可以成为更清洁体系的一部分，但只有当我们对比碳数字比对时髦分子更加忠诚时才是如此。

燃料不是一个道德范畴；它是一串转变。如果那一链条是清洁的、谨慎的，并被保留给它真正能做好的工作，氢就会帮助气候。 💧

questions.q: 1. Why is hydrogen “only as clean as the method used to produce it”?
options: Because it cannot be used in any fuel cell
Because hydrogen never binds to other atoms on Earth
Because most hydrogen from gas releases carbon dioxide unless captured, and electricity-based hydrogen is clean only if the electricity is low-carbon
Because color labels prove automatic virtue
questions.exp: 来源决定清洁程度：天然气制氢会排碳，电解氢的清洁取决于电力是否低碳。

questions.q: 2. Where is hydrogen described as more useful than as a universal home or car fuel?
options: In every home heating system without exception
As a cheap replacement for all infrastructure
Where slogans already solved leakage
In some heavy transport, high-temperature industry, and long-duration storage, because batteries struggle there and conversion losses are large elsewhere
questions.exp: 氢在重型运输、高温工业和长时储能等电池吃力的地方更有用。

questions.q: 3. Why do leakage and safety matter beyond fire risk?
options: Because engineering is unnecessary if slogans are strong
Because trade will not change geopolitics
Because hydrogen cannot escape pipes
Because leaked hydrogen can be an indirect greenhouse issue by affecting other gases in the atmosphere
questions.exp: 大量泄漏会通过影响大气中其他气体而成为间接温室问题。

questions.q: 4. What “boring, essential questions” should the public ask?
options: Whether a single molecule can be a universal hero
Whether workers in old fuel industries need no transition
How the hydrogen was made, how much energy was lost, who pays for infrastructure, and who benefits
Whether silence in an advertisement is always reassuring
questions.exp: 应问氢如何制成、沿途损失多少能量、谁为基础设施付钱、谁受益。

questions.q: 5. What comparison exercise is suggested?
options: Accept “hydrogen economy” as a phrase that can greenwash anything
Compare a hydrogen plan and a battery plan for a specific use and list advantages honestly
Treat fashionable molecules as more important than carbon numbers
Ignore the electricity or gas behind a “green” label
questions.exp: 就公交、钢厂或无风冬季周等具体用途比较氢与电池，并诚实列出优势。

senior.title: ⏳ Planned Obsolescence: When Products Are Designed to Be Temporary
senior.content:
Some objects wear out honestly, after a long life of use. Others seem to fail just after a warranty ends, or become unusable because software support is withdrawn, or because a single unreplaceable part dies. Planned obsolescence is the suspicion, and sometimes the documented practice, that a product’s short life is not an accident but a design choice. In a culture of upgrades, it can be hard to tell misfortune from strategy, which is exactly why the question matters. Companies may shorten a product’s life to sell the next model, to cut production costs, or to keep a service subscription necessary. Methods range from fragile parts and sealed batteries to software that slows older devices or refuses new applications. Not every failure is a conspiracy; materials have limits, and innovation really does improve some tools. A serious critique looks for patterns, not for a villain in every broken toaster.

The environmental bill is large. Mining, manufacturing, and shipping a replacement phone or appliance use energy and minerals that a longer-lived object would have saved. E-waste then piles up, often in places far from the comfortable rooms where the device was first unboxed. A short product life is a long chain of hidden harm. Consumers are not powerless, but they are busy and poorly informed. Labels that state expected lifetimes, a right to repair, and the ability to keep using a device after official updates end can shift power back toward owners. Reputation can also punish firms, if buyers can actually see which brands last.

There is a psychological side. Marketing teaches people to feel embarrassed by a working object that is merely unfashionable. Even a durable phone can be abandoned because a camera or a shape has become a social signal. Planned obsolescence then partners with cultural obsolescence, and both need to be questioned. Lawmakers in several regions have begun to regulate misleading durability claims and to require spare parts for a number of years. Enforcement will decide whether the rules are theater. Designers, for their part, can treat longevity as a mark of quality rather than as a threat to last quarter’s sales.

Students can practice a slower kind of shopping: asking how long a device should reasonably last, whether it can be opened, and whether they are replacing something that still works because of ads rather than need. The questions sound unglamorous. They are a form of environmental and civic literacy. Take one object you recently replaced and write two columns: what actually failed, and what still worked. Then ask whether a part, a policy, or a feeling of being outdated caused the change. Planned obsolescence is easiest to accept when we do not inspect our own closets. Inspection is the beginning of refusing to be designed as a permanent customer.

A product that cannot last is teaching its owner a lesson about waste and about power. The lesson can be accepted, or it can be answered with better design, better law, and a less obedient appetite for the next new thing. ⏳
senior.translation:
有些物品在长久使用之后诚实地磨损。另一些似乎刚好在保修结束之后失灵，或因为软件支持被撤回，或因为一个无法更换的零件死去，而变得无法使用。计划性过时是一种怀疑，有时也是被记录下来的做法：一件产品的短寿并不是意外，而是一种设计选择。在升级文化里，很难分清不幸与策略，而这正是这个问题之所以重要的原因。 公司可能缩短产品寿命以销售下一款、削减生产成本，或使服务订阅成为必要。方法从易碎零件和密封电池，到使旧设备变慢或拒绝新应用的软件。并非每一次故障都是阴谋；材料有限度，创新也的确改进了一些工具。严肃的批评寻找模式，而不是在每一台坏掉的烤面包机里寻找恶棍。

环境账单是巨大的。采矿、制造和运输一部替换手机或电器，使用着一件更长寿的物品本可以节省的能源和矿物。电子废物随后堆积起来，常常堆在远离设备第一次被打开的舒适房间的地方。短暂的产品生命，是一长串隐藏的伤害。 消费者并非无能为力，但他们很忙，且信息不足。标明预期寿命的标签、维修权，以及在官方更新结束后仍能继续使用设备的能力，可以把权力移回所有者。如果买家真正能看见哪些品牌更耐用，声誉也可以惩罚公司。

这里有心理的一面。营销教人们为一件仍然能用、只是不再时髦的物品感到尴尬。即使一部耐用的手机也可能被放弃，因为一个摄像头或一种外形变成了社会信号。计划性过时于是与文化过时合伙，两者都需要被质疑。 一些地区的立法者已开始规范误导性的耐用声明，并要求在若干年内提供备件。执行将决定这些规则是不是剧场。设计师这一边，可以把长寿当作质量的标记，而不是对上一季度销量的威胁。

学生可以练习一种更慢的购物：询问一件设备合理地应当用多久，它是否能被打开，以及他们是否因为广告而不是需要，正在替换一件仍然能用的东西。这些问题听起来不起眼。它们是一种环境和公民素养。 拿一件你最近更换的物品，写两栏：实际坏了的是什么，仍然能用的是什么。然后再问导致更换的是一个零件、一项政策，还是一种过时了的感觉。当我们不检查自己的柜子时，计划性过时最容易被接受。检查，就是拒绝被设计成永久顾客的开始。

一件不能持久的产品，正在向它的主人讲授关于浪费和权力的一课。这一课可以被接受，也可以用更好的设计、更好的法律，以及一种不那么顺从的、对下一件新东西的胃口来回答。 ⏳

Replace every working object because of ads

senior.title: 🔬 The Gender Gap in STEM: Talent Is Not the Scarce Resource
senior.content:
In many countries, girls now match or outpace boys in school science and mathematics, yet women remain underrepresented in some branches of engineering, physics, and technology careers. The pattern is not a simple story of ability, and it is not the same in every subject or culture. Explaining the STEM gender gap requires looking at stereotypes, workplaces, role models, and the quiet ways a classroom can signal who “belongs.” Talent is abundant. Belonging and fair conditions are often what run short. Stereotypes begin early. Toys, media, and casual comments can teach children that brilliance in certain fields is a male trait, even when teachers officially disagree. Girls may then need more evidence that they are “allowed” to be excellent, or they may avoid a subject after a single discouraging moment that a boy would treat as ordinary friction.

Secondary and university pathways matter. If advanced classes, internships, and informal networks are dominated by one group, equally prepared students can still drift away. A lab culture of late-night heroics, sexist jokes, or harassment is not a side issue; it is a filter that has nothing to do with equations. Some arguments point to average differences in interests. Even if interests are not identical on average, the overlap is huge, and interest itself is shaped by what a society praises. Using a small average difference to justify a huge career gap is a statistical and moral mistake.

Policy and practice can change outcomes: visible role models, fair hiring, parental leave, and teaching that treats struggle as normal for everyone. Special programs can help, provided they do not become a substitute for fixing the mainstream environment. A scholarship cannot cancel a hostile workplace. Men and boys are not the enemy of the analysis. Many are allies, and some fields have other diversity problems that also deserve attention, including class and race. The goal is not a ritual of blame, but a more accurate map of wasted potential.

Students can watch their own classrooms for small signals: who is asked the hard question, who is interrupted, whose project is called “ambitious.” Those moments look minor in a single hour. Over years they become a career. Talk with someone in a STEM field about a moment when they felt they belonged, or did not, and listen for the conditions around that moment—not only for their private feelings. Then look at your school’s advanced classes and ask who is missing. The gender gap in STEM is a reminder that a society can officially love science and still build rooms in which only some kinds of people feel permitted to stay.

A wasted mind is a public loss, not a private disappointment. Closing the gap is less about inventing new talent than about stopping a thousand small doors from closing on talent that already exists. 🔬
senior.translation:
在许多国家，女孩在学校科学和数学上现在已经赶上或超过男孩，然而在工程、物理和科技职业的某些分支，女性仍然代表性不足。这一模式不是一个关于能力的简单故事，在每一个科目或文化中也不相同。解释STEM性别差距，需要审视刻板印象、工作场所、榜样，以及一间教室可以用来暗示谁“属于这里”的安静方式。才能是丰富的。常常短缺的，是归属感和公平的条件。 刻板印象开始得很早。玩具、媒体和随口评论可以教给孩子，某些领域的聪慧是男性特质，即使教师在官方上不同意。女孩随后可能需要更多证据来证明她们“被允许”优秀，或在一次泄气的瞬间之后避开一门科目，而一个男孩会把同样的瞬间当成普通的摩擦。

中学和大学的路径很重要。如果高级课程、实习和非正式网络被一个群体主导，同样有准备的学生仍可能漂走。一种深夜英雄主义、性别歧视笑话或骚扰的实验室文化，不是边角问题；它是一个与方程式无关的过滤器。 有些论点指向兴趣上的平均差异。即使平均兴趣并不完全相同，重叠也是巨大的，而且兴趣本身会被一个社会赞美什么所塑造。用一个小小的平均差异为巨大的职业差距辩护，是统计上和道德上的错误。

政策与实践可以改变结果：可见的榜样、公平的招聘、育儿假，以及把挣扎当作对每个人都正常的教学。特别项目可以有帮助，只要它们不成为修复主流环境的替代品。一份奖学金不能取消一个充满敌意的工作场所。 男性和男孩并不是这一分析的敌人。许多人是同盟，而且有些领域还有包括阶级和种族在内的、同样值得注意的其他多样性问题。目标不是一场责备的仪式，而是一张关于被浪费潜力的更准确的地图。

学生可以在他们自己的教室里观察小信号：谁被问到难题，谁被打断，谁的项目被称为“有雄心”。那些时刻在单一小时里看起来很小。多年之后，它们会变成一份职业。 与一位STEM领域的人交谈，询问他们感到自己属于或不属于的一个时刻，并倾听那一时刻周围的条件——而不仅仅是他们的私人感受。然后再看你学校的高级课程，询问谁缺席了。STEM中的性别差距提醒我们：一个社会可以在官方上热爱科学，却仍然建造只有某些人感到被允许留下的房间。

一颗被浪费的心智是公共损失，不是私人失望。缩小差距，与其说是发明新的才能，不如说是阻止一千扇小门在已经存在的才能面前关上。 🔬

senior.title: ➗ Fair Division: The Mathematics of Sharing Without a Fight
senior.content:
Sharing a cake, a set of rooms, or a common budget sounds like a moral problem, and it is. It is also a mathematical one. Fair-division theory studies rules that can give people shares they have reason to accept, even when they value the same objects differently. The subject is more than a party trick. It trains a way of thinking about justice that does not depend only on shouting that one is right. A simple method for two people and a heterogeneous cake is “I cut, you choose.” The cutter, fearing the worse piece, has an incentive to make the shares equal in their own eyes; the chooser then takes the piece they prefer. The result is envy-free for two, in a precise sense: neither prefers the other’s piece to their own.

With three or more people, or with objects that cannot be sliced, the problem becomes harder. Methods exist—some using moving knives, lists of preferences, or random lotteries combined with guarantees—but each method satisfies some fairness properties and not others. You may be able to avoid envy, or to ensure that everyone gets at least 1/n of the total in their own measure, but not always both, and not always with a procedure people will actually follow. The theory is honest about impossibility. Some combinations of desirable properties cannot be satisfied at once, just as some voting systems cannot meet every democratic wish. Knowing this can lower the temperature of a dispute: the argument may be about which fairness we are choosing, not about who is secretly evil.

Applications appear in inheritance, divorce, land, airport landing slots, and the allocation of household chores. In each case, people often begin with a vague cry of “be fair,” then discover that they meant different things: equal amounts, equal satisfaction, priority for the neediest, or compensation for past harm. Mathematics cannot pick the moral goal, but it can show which rules serve which goal. There is a classroom gift in this. Students who fear that ethics is only opinion, or that mathematics is only abstract, meet a topic in which numbers and values have to talk to each other. A clean procedure will not heal every family argument, yet it can replace a shouting match with a transparent rule.

Skeptics say that real people will still cheat, or that feelings cannot be captured by a diagram. They are partly right. A fair rule still needs good information and a willingness to abide by an outcome. The mathematics is a tool for honest people, not a spell that removes the need for honesty. Try the cut-and-choose method with a classmate over something that can actually be divided, and then try to describe what would go wrong with a third person. If you prefer a less sticky example, allocate three different chores for a week using a written preference list. Fair division is civics with a pencil. It shows that “share nicely” is the beginning of a problem, not the end of one.

Justice often fails not only because people are greedy, but because they are vague. A better rule will not make us saints, but it can make our disagreements sharper, fairer, and sometimes shorter. ➗
senior.translation:
分享一块蛋糕、一套房间或一笔共同预算，听起来像一个道德问题，而它也是。它也是一个数学问题。公平分割理论研究一些规则，使人有理由接受自己的份额，即使他们对同样的物品评价不同。这个主题不只是宴会上的把戏。它训练一种思考正义的方式，这种方式并不仅仅依赖于高喊自己是对的。 对两个人和一块不均匀的蛋糕，一个简单方法是“我切你选”。切的人害怕更差的一块，就有激励在自己眼中把份额切得相等；选的人随后拿走自己更偏好的一块。结果在一种精确的意义上对两个人都是无嫉妒的：谁也不更喜欢对方的那一块胜过自己的。

当有三人或更多人，或物品不能被切开时，问题就变得更难。方法是存在的——有些使用移动的刀、偏好清单，或与保证相结合的随机抽签——但每一种方法满足某些公平性质而不满足另一些。你也许能够避免嫉妒，或确保每个人按自己的度量至少得到总量的1/n，但并不总是两者都能，也并不总是有一个人们真正会遵循的程序。 这一理论对不可能性是诚实的。某些理想性质的组合不能被同时满足，正如某些选举制度不能满足每一种民主愿望。知道这一点可以降低争执的温度：争论可能是关于我们在选择哪一种公平，而不是关于谁在暗中作恶。

应用出现在继承、离婚、土地、机场起降时段和家务分配中。在每一种情形里，人们常常从一句模糊的“要公平”开始，然后发现他们指的是不同的东西：相等的数量、相等的满意度、优先给最需要的人，或对过去伤害的补偿。数学不能挑选道德目标，但它可以表明哪些规则服务哪些目标。 这里有一份课堂礼物。那些担心伦理只是意见、或数学只是抽象的学生，会遇到一个数字与价值必须彼此交谈的主题。一个干净的程序不会治愈每一个家庭争论，但它可以用一条透明的规则替换一场叫骂。

怀疑者说，真实的人仍会作弊，或者感觉无法被一张图捕捉。他们有一部分是对的。一条公平的规则仍然需要良好的信息和遵守结果的意愿。数学是给诚实者的工具，不是消除对诚实之需要的咒语。 与同学用真正可以分割的东西试一下“我切你选”，然后再试着说明第三个人会出什么问题。如果你更喜欢不那么黏的例子，用一份书面偏好清单来分配一周里三件不同的家务。公平分割是带着一支铅笔的公民课。它表明“好好分享”是一个问题的开始，而不是结束。

正义常常失败，不仅因为人贪婪，也因为人含糊。一条更好的规则不会使我们成为圣人，但它可以使我们的分歧更锐利、更公平，有时也更短。 ➗

senior.title: 👥 Peer Tutoring: Learning Twice by Teaching Once
senior.content:
A student who has just mastered a topic is sometimes a better explainer, for a classmate, than a distant expert. Peer tutoring organizes that possibility: one student helps another under the school’s responsibility, not as a chaotic replacement for teaching. Done well, it can raise understanding, confidence, and the feeling that knowledge is a shared project. Done badly, it can become unpaid labor, a way to hide teacher shortages, or an embarrassing public display of who is “slow.” The learning benefit often goes in both directions. The tutor must reorganize knowledge, find new examples, and notice holes in their own understanding—a process sometimes called the protege effect. The learner may ask the “obvious” questions that a classroom moved past too quickly, and may feel safer taking a risk with a near-age partner than with an adult.

Structure is essential. Tutors need a little training: how to wait, how to ask rather than simply tell, how to keep dignity intact, and when to call a teacher. Sessions should have a clear goal and a limited time, so that friendship is not confused with a permanent hierarchy of clever and weak. Equity problems appear immediately. If only high-scoring students tutor, and only in ways that add to their university applications, the program can widen status gaps. Rotating roles, tutoring in different subjects, and recognizing many kinds of strength—language, patience, practical skill—can spread honor more fairly.

Teachers remain central. Peer tutoring cannot diagnose every misconception or replace professional planning. It is a supplement, like a well-run study group with a purpose, and it works best when the adult still designs the sequence and checks the results. There is a social education as well. Students practice explaining without humiliating, and asking for help without shame. Those habits matter in workplaces and in civic life, where people must continually teach and be taught by equals.

Online tools can extend tutoring across distance, and they can also reduce it to copied answers. The value lies in the dialogue, not in a finished worksheet that appears by magic. A school that cares about integrity will watch for that difference. Offer to explain one problem you understand to a classmate, or ask for an explanation of one you do not, and then write down what changed in your own head. Notice whether the tone was respectful. Peer tutoring, at its best, is not a ladder of rank. It is a reminder that a class is smarter as a network than as a row of isolated competitors.

Teaching a peer is a test of whether you really understand, and of whether you can be generous with what you know. A school that makes room for both tests is teaching more than a syllabus. 👥
senior.translation:
一个刚刚掌握某个主题的学生，对同学而言，有时是比一位遥远专家更好的解释者。同伴辅导把这种可能组织起来：一名学生在学校的责任之下帮助另一名学生，而不是作为教学的混乱替代。做得好，它可以提升理解、信心，以及知识是一项共享事业的感觉。做得不好，它可以变成无酬劳动、掩盖教师短缺的方式，或一场关于谁“慢”的尴尬公开展示。 学习收益常常是双向的。辅导者必须重新组织知识，找到新的例子，并注意到自己理解中的漏洞——这一过程有时被称为被指导者效应。学习者可能问出课堂跳得太快的“显而易见”的问题，并且与一个年龄接近的伙伴冒险，可能比与一个成人更有安全感。

结构是必要的。辅导者需要一点训练：如何等待，如何提问而不是只是告诉，如何保持尊严完整，以及何时叫老师。辅导应当有清晰目标和有限时间，这样友谊才不会与聪明和软弱的永久等级混淆。 公平问题立刻出现。如果只有高分学生辅导，并且只以增加他们大学申请的方式进行，项目就可能扩大地位差距。轮换角色、在不同科目中辅导，以及承认许多种类的长处——语言、耐心、实践技能——可以更公平地分配荣誉。

教师仍然是核心。同伴辅导不能诊断每一种误解，或替代专业的规划。它是一种补充，像一个有目的、运行良好的学习小组，而当成人仍然设计顺序并检查结果时，它运作得最好。 这里也有社会教育。学生练习在不羞辱的情况下解释，以及在不羞耻的情况下求助。那些习惯在工作场所和公民生活中很重要，在那里人们必须不断地教平等的人，也被平等的人教。

在线工具可以把辅导延伸到远距离，也可以把它减成抄来的答案。价值在于对话，而不在于一份神奇出现的完成作业。一所关心诚信的学校会注意这一差别。 主动向同学解释一道你懂的题，或请人解释一道你不懂的题，然后写下你自己头脑里什么发生了变化。注意语气是否尊重。同伴辅导在最好的时候，不是一架等级梯子。它提醒我们：一个班级作为网络，比作为一排孤立的竞争者更聪明。

教一名同伴，是对你是否真正理解，以及你能否对自己所知保持慷慨的一次检验。一所为这两种检验都留出空间的学校，教的就不只是一份大纲。 👥

senior.title: 🧴 Everyday Chemicals: Useful, Invisible, and in Need of a Calm Kind of Caution
senior.content:
Modern life is soaked in chemistry that our great-grandparents would not have recognized: stain removers, flame retardants, cosmetics, food packaging, and the coatings inside cans. Many of these substances make life safer, cheaper, or more convenient. A smaller number are later found to persist in bodies and ecosystems, or to interfere with hormones at low doses. The adult response is neither panic about every bottle nor a naive trust that “if it is sold, it must be harmless.” It is a calm demand for evidence, labels, and substitutes when risk is real. Exposure often happens in tiny amounts over years, which makes cause and effect hard to see in daily life. Scientists use toxicology, epidemiology, and animal or cell studies, each with limits. A chemical that is dangerous in a factory spill may be trivial in a trace on a package, or the reverse may be true if the substance accumulates or acts during a sensitive period of development.

Regulation tries to keep up, and frequently lags. A product can be legal for a long time before independent research catches a problem, especially when thousands of substances are in use and testing is expensive. The precautionary principle—acting to reduce exposure when serious harm is plausible but not fully proven—remains controversial, because it can also block useful innovations. Consumers can lower some risks in modest ways: ventilating while cleaning, choosing unscented or simpler products, reducing unnecessary plastics in food, and not assuming that “natural” always means safer. Personal action has limits. A renter cannot redesign a building’s materials, and a child cannot choose the air in a classroom.

Industry has knowledge and also a conflict of interest. Responsible firms test and reformulate; others wait for scandal. Public laboratories, journalists, and clear rules about what must be disclosed are therefore part of chemical safety, not optional extras. There is an environmental justice dimension. Communities near plants, waste sites, or busy roads often receive a heavier chemical load, while advertising for “pure” lifestyles is aimed at those who can already buy their way toward lower exposure. A fair policy looks at the neighborhood, not only at the shopping basket.

Students can practice reading an ingredient list and a reliable public-health page together, rather than a frightened video. Chemical literacy is the habit of asking “how much, for whom, and for how long?” instead of “is this substance evil?” Pick one product you use every week and try to find a trustworthy source on its main chemicals—not a sales page and not a rumor. Notice what is known, what is still uncertain, and what a regulator has already decided. Everyday chemistry is a test of maturity: the ability to live with useful tools without pretending that risk is either zero or everywhere.

We will not return to a world without synthetic chemistry, and we should not want a world that refuses to inspect it. Caution, in this field, is a form of respect for bodies that cannot easily opt out of the modern material world. 🧴
senior.translation:
现代生活浸泡在我们的曾祖父母可能认不出的化学之中：去污剂、阻燃剂、化妆品、食品包装，以及罐头内壁的涂层。这些物质中的许多使生活更安全、更便宜或更方便。较小的一部分后来被发现会在身体和生态系统中持久存在，或在低剂量下干扰激素。成人的反应既不是对每一个瓶子的恐慌，也不是天真地相信“只要在售，就一定无害”。它是在风险真实时，对证据、标签和替代品的平静要求。 暴露常常以多年中的微量发生，这使得因果关系在日常生活中难以看见。科学家使用毒理学、流行病学以及动物或细胞研究，每一种都有限度。一种在工厂泄漏中危险的化学品，在包装上的痕迹里可能微不足道；反过来也可能为真，如果该物质会累积，或在发育的敏感时期起作用。

监管试图跟上，并常常滞后。一件产品可以在独立研究抓住问题之前合法很长时间，尤其当使用中的物质以千计、而测试又昂贵时。预防原则——在严重伤害看似可能但尚未被完全证明时采取行动以减少暴露——仍然有争议，因为它也可能阻挡有用的创新。 消费者可以用谦逊的方式降低某些风险：清洁时通风，选择无香或更简单的产品，减少食物中不必要的塑料，并且不假定“天然”总是意味着更安全。个人行动是有限度的。租客不能重新设计一栋楼的材料，孩子也不能选择教室里的空气。

产业拥有知识，也拥有利益冲突。负责任的公司会测试并重新配方；另一些则等待丑闻。公共实验室、记者，以及关于必须披露什么的清晰规则，因此是化学品安全的一部分，不是可选的附加。 这里有环境正义的一面。工厂、废物场或繁忙道路附近的社区常常承受更重的化学负荷，而“纯净”生活方式的广告却瞄准那些已经能花钱走向更低暴露的人。公平的政策看街区，而不仅仅看购物篮。

学生可以练习把一份成分表和一页可靠的公共卫生资料一起阅读，而不是看一个惊恐的视频。化学素养是询问“多少、对谁、多久？”而不是“这种物质是恶的吗？”的习惯。 选一件你每周都使用的产品，试着找到关于其主要化学物质的可信来源——不是销售页，也不是谣言。注意什么是已知的，什么仍然不确定，以及监管者已经决定了什么。日常化学是对成熟的一次检验：在有用的工具中生活，而不假装风险要么为零，要么无处不在。

我们不会回到一个没有合成化学的世界，也不应当想要一个拒绝检查它的世界。在这个领域，谨慎是对那些不容易退出现代物质世界的身体的一种尊重。 🧴
